title: Episode 99: The Great Boston Molasses Flood of 1919: The Deadly Tidal Wave of Treacle
description:
On January 15, 1919, a colossal fifty-foot steel tank in Boston's North End ruptured, unleashing a twenty-five-foot wave of two million gallons of molasses moving at thirty-five miles per hour. The sticky tsunami killed twenty-one people and injured one hundred and fifty.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we visit the historic North End of Boston, Massachusetts, on an unusually mild winter afternoon in January nineteen nineteen, to witness one of the strangest, deadliest, and most surreal industrial disasters in American history: the Great Boston Molasses Flood. In the heart of an Italian immigrant neighborhood, a massive, poorly constructed fifty-foot steel storage tank held over two million gallons of dark industrial molasses, destined to be distilled into munitions alcohol for World War I. When structural fatigue and winter fermentation caused the tank to violently rupture, an avalanche of two-point-three million gallons of molasses surged through the streets at thirty-five miles per hour, demolishing buildings, lifting streetcars, and suffocating twenty-one people in a terrifying brown tsunami. Here is George with the full, astonishing story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: INDUSTRIAL MOLASSES AND THE NORTH END
In the early twentieth century, Boston's North End was a vibrant, densely populated working-class enclave of Italian and Irish immigrant families. Amidst the narrow cobblestone streets, tenement houses, and bakery storefronts stood the busy commercial waterfront of Boston Harbor. In nineteen fifteen, the United States Industrial Alcohol Company—known as USIA—constructed a colossal steel storage tank on Commercial Street, just steps from the Boston Elevated Railway and the crowded wharves.
The tank was a gargantuan cylinder measuring fifty feet tall and ninety feet in diameter, capable of holding nearly two and a half million gallons. It was built for a single, highly lucrative wartime purpose: storing raw fermented molasses imported from Puerto Rico, Cuba, and the West Indies. While modern consumers think of molasses primarily as a sweet syrup for baking, industrial molasses was a strategic chemical commodity during World War I. By distilling molasses into industrial ethanol, USIA produced alcohol essential for the manufacture of smokeless gunpowder, cordite, dynamite, and high explosives for Allied armies on the Western Front.
Furthermore, with the looming passage of the Eighteenth Amendment establishing national Prohibition, USIA was racing against the clock in early nineteen nineteen to import as much molasses as possible and distill it into potable alcohol before the nation went legally dry. Financial greed and wartime urgency combined to push production to the absolute limit, with corporate executives turning a blind eye to the lethal time bomb ticking on the Boston waterfront. Wartime munitions contracts generated enormous profits for alcohol distillers, encouraging corporations to disregard basic safety protocols.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE SINS OF THE STEEL MONSTER
From the very day it was constructed in nineteen fifteen, the USIA molasses tank was an engineering catastrophe waiting to happen. To rush construction, corporate treasurer Arthur P. Jell had supervised the project without consulting qualified structural engineers, naval architects, or city building inspectors. The steel plates used for the tank walls were dangerously thin—measuring only a fraction of the thickness required to hold the immense hydrostatic pressure of two million gallons of molasses, which is forty percent denser than water, weighing nearly twelve pounds per gallon.
Even worse, the rivets holding the curved steel plates together were undersized and spaced too far apart. When the tank was first filled with a modest test batch of water, leaks appeared immediately along the seams, but USIA officials refused to perform a full hydrostatic pressure test, dismissing the defects as minor blemishes. As successive shipments of thick molasses were pumped into the tank over the next three years, the structure groaned, shuddered, and leaked continuously.
Neighborhood children routinely collected jars of sticky brown molasses dripping from the leaking seams, and local workers dipped their sticks into puddles along the sidewalk. Rather than draining the tank, replacing the rivets, and reinforcing the steel walls, USIA management adopted an insulting cosmetic cover-up: they ordered the entire steel tank painted a dark, mottled reddish-brown so that the chronic leaking molasses would not be visible to the public or municipal authorities. Corporate executives prioritized industrial output over human life, ignoring repeated warning signs and worker complaints for three years.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE UNSEASONABLE THAW AND THE RUPTURE
In early January nineteen nineteen, the lethal trap was finally sprung by the New England weather. On January twelfth, a steamship arrived from Puerto Rico and pumped over two million gallons of freshly brewed, warm tropical molasses directly into the Commercial Street tank, bringing the total volume to an astonishing two million three hundred thousand gallons—filling the tank nearly to its fifty-foot brim.
For the next two days, the warm Caribbean molasses mingled with the cold, viscous molasses already sitting in the tank. Then, on Tuesday and Wednesday, January fourteenth and fifteenth, a dramatic winter weather shift struck Boston. Temperatures leaped from a bitter two degrees below zero up to an unseasonably warm forty-three degrees Fahrenheit. This rapid forty-five-degree temperature change triggered intense internal fermentation within the molasses, generating vast quantities of trapped carbon dioxide gas that exerted immense pneumatic pressure against the already stressed, paper-thin steel roof and walls.
At twelve forty on the afternoon of Wednesday, January fifteenth, workers along Commercial Street were sitting outside eating lunch in the mild winter air, children were playing in the streets, and freight handlers were loading wagons on the wharves. Deep inside the tank, the sound of machine-gun-like popping began as over-stressed steel rivets sheared off in rapid succession. Then, with a deafening roar that witnesses described as a cross between a thunderclap and an artillery bombardment, the giant tank ruptured. The sudden temperature spike catalyzed an explosive biochemical reaction that the fatally under-engineered steel walls could not contain.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE TWENTY-FIVE-FOOT TSUNAMI
The colossal failure of the steel tank unleashed a horrific physical phenomenon that nobody could have imagined: a twenty-five-foot-high, one-hundred-and-sixty-foot-wide tidal wave of dark, boiling molasses surging through the streets at thirty-five miles per hour. Weighing twelve thousand tons, the moving wall of viscous fluid possessed staggering kinetic energy, moving with the destructive power of a solid concrete ram.
The wave slammed into the nearby Boston Elevated Railway trestle, ripping out heavy steel support girders as if they were matchsticks. An elevated passenger train was approaching the station when the tracks ahead collapsed; the heroic motorman threw the emergency brakes just in time, bringing the front car to a halt dangling precariously over the surging sea of molasses below. On the street level, the two-story North End firehouse was ripped completely off its foundation and pushed fifty feet into Boston Harbor, with firefighters trapped in the attic.
Tenement buildings, freight offices, and warehouses were pulverized within seconds. Giant jagged shards of the ruptured steel tank, weighing several tons each, were hurled through the air like shrapnel, slicing through telephone poles and slicing into adjacent homes. A two-ton chunk of steel was blown across the street and buried into an electric substation, severing power lines and igniting fires in the flooded ruins. The kinetic momentum of twelve thousand tons of boiling syrup pulverized heavy infrastructure with the unstoppable fury of an avalanche.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE SUFFOCATING NIGHTMARE
For the pedestrians, horses, and workers caught in the path of the wave, survival was a desperate, horrific struggle against an impossible enemy. Unlike water, which flows away and allows victims to swim, molasses is an ultra-viscous, non-Newtonian fluid. As victims struggled to move, the fluid's viscosity increased, locking their arms and legs in an inescapable, suffocating grip like wet concrete.
Dozens of people were knocked down and instantly submerged beneath two to three feet of thick, choking syrup. Those who managed to raise their heads found their mouths, nostrils, and eyes clogged by the sticky mass, suffocating them where they lay. Ten-year-old Maria Distasio and her friend Pasquale Iantosca were walking home from school when the wave engulfed them; both died within minutes. Teamsters and their heavy draft horses were trapped in the streets; over twenty horses were so deeply mired and thrashing in panic that police officers were forced to shoot them to end their suffering.
The first responders on the scene were one hundred and sixteen naval cadets from the training ship USS Nantucket, docked nearby. Commanded by Lieutenant Commander H. J. Copeland, the young sailors sprinted into the waist-deep morass of molasses, forming human chains to haul semi-conscious victims from the wreckage. Boston police officers, firemen, and Red Cross volunteers arrived shortly after, but walking through the cooling syrup was nearly impossible; rescuers were exhausted within minutes, their boots pulled off by the suction of the cooling treacle. Naval cadets and city responders performed superhuman rescue feats, pulling drowning children from the cooling, suffocating morass.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE CLEAN-UP AND THE BITTER STENCH
When the rescue operations finally concluded days later, the human toll stood at twenty-one dead and one hundred and fifty injured. Many of the bodies were recovered days later, so thoroughly coated in hardened molasses that they were unrecognizable, requiring dental records and personal rings for identification. The final victim, a wagon driver named Cesare Nicolo, was pulled from the waters beneath the harbor wharves nearly four months after the disaster.
The cleanup of the North End was an epic, miserable labor that took months. The cold winter weather caused the molasses to congeal into a thick, rubbery crust that resisted brooms, shovels, and pickaxes. City engineers finally realized that ordinary fresh water was useless; they brought in city fireboats to pump millions of gallons of pressurized saltwater from the harbor, which dissolved the sticky sugar and washed the sludge into the sea, turning Boston Harbor brown for weeks.
Meanwhile, the disaster spread throughout the metropolitan area on the shoes of thousands of spectators, rescue workers, and commuters. Molasses was tracked onto streetcars, subway seats, telephone booths, and living room carpets across Boston. For decades afterward, residents claimed that on hot, humid summer days, the unmistakable, sweet, cloying aroma of fermented molasses would still rise from the cobblestones and basements of the North End. Saltwater from harbor fireboats proved the only effective solvent against the congealing sugar, which coated neighborhoods for months.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE LANDMARK TRIAL AND CORPORATE ACCOUNTABILITY
In the immediate aftermath of the catastrophe, the United States Industrial Alcohol Company attempted to evade all financial and moral responsibility by concocting an elaborate defense: they claimed that the tank had been deliberately blown up by Italian anarchists and foreign saboteurs. During the height of the Red Scare, USIA pointed to recent anarchist bombings in New York and Boston, hiring private detectives to find evidence of dynamite residue.
However, in nineteen twenty, the victims and their families consolidated their lawsuits in the first massive class-action tort proceeding in Massachusetts history, appointing former state auditor Hugh W. Ogden as the special court auditor to hear evidence. Over the course of three grueling years, Ogden presided over one of the longest and most thorough trials in American legal history, hearing testimony from over nine hundred witnesses and filling twenty-five thousand pages of transcripts.
In nineteen twenty-five, Ogden delivered a blistering, historic ruling that completely dismissed the anarchist sabotage theory. He found USIA solely guilty of gross corporate negligence, proving that the tank was structurally defective, constructed with substandard steel, and overloaded beyond its physical limits. USIA was ordered to pay three hundred thousand dollars in damages—equivalent to nearly five million dollars today—to the victims and their families.
The Great Boston Molasses Flood fundamentally transformed American industrial safety and municipal governance. In its wake, the City of Boston and municipalities across the nation enacted revolutionary building code reforms, mandating that all commercial structures and storage tanks undergo rigorous engineering inspections, hydrostatic testing, and formal sign-offs by certified professional engineers. Today, a modest green plaque on the Boston Harborwalk marks the site of the vanished tank, an enduring reminder of twenty-one innocent lives lost to corporate greed and the day Boston drowned in molasses. The landmark legal victory held industrial corporations strictly liable for public safety, establishing modern architectural and municipal engineering standards.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Boston Molasses Flood revolutionized municipal engineering oversight and established modern corporate liability for public safety. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we ascend into the Green Mountains of Vermont for Ethan Allen's daring dawn raid on Fort Ticonderoga.
